div.p: Maximum likelihood (ML) estimation of spatial autoregressive models for large spatial data sets is well established by making use of the commonly sparse nature of the contiguity matrix on which spatial dependence is built. Adding a measurement error that naturally separates the spatial process from the measurement error process are not well established in the literature, however, and ML estimation of such models to large data sets is challenging. Recently a reduced rank approach was suggested which re-expresses and approximates such a model as a spatial random effects model (SRE) in order to achieve fast fitting of large data sets by fitting the corresponding SRE. In this paper we propose a fast and exact method to accomplish ML estimation and restricted ML estimation of complexity of O(n 3/2 ) operations when the contiguity matrix is based on a local neighbourhood. The methods are illustrated using the well known data set on house prices in Lucas County in Ohio.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Simultaneous autoregressive (SAR) models and the larger class of spatial econometric models are popular regression models which take the spatial dependence of units into account (Lesage and Pace 2009). There are two main SAR models, one where the spatial dependence is directly incorporated into the equation for the response variable, here referred to as the spatial lag model (SLM), and a model where the spatial dependence is incorporated into the error term, the spatial error model (SEM). Another popular model approach is the so-called conditional autoregressive (CAR) model, see Cressie (1993) for details.

Maximum likelihood (ML) estimation of the SLM and the SEM is well known and has been studied by Ord (1975) using the eigenvalues of the contiguity matrix W which avoids the repeated calculation of the determinant in the optimisation process. Many software packages, such as the R package spdep (Bivand 2017), use these methods to achieve ML estimation. For large data sets and sparse contiguity matrices, the calculation of eigenvalues is often avoided and the repeated calculation of the determinant is preferred, because in this case the repeated calculation of the determinant is usually much quicker than the calculation of the eigenvalues.

There are many extensions of these SAR models, for example a model including spatially lagged covariates, the so-called SLX model, the spatial Durbin model (SDM) and the spatial Durbin error model (SDEM). For an overview of various spatial econometric models and extensions, see for example Lesage and Pace (2009), Halleck Vega and Elhorst (2015), Bivand and Piras (2015) and LeSage et al. (2017).

Often variables are measured with different types of errors, often referred to as measurement error. For example when observed covariates contain such a measurement error, then the fixed effects estimates referring to the covariate without measurement error are biased (Huque et al. 2014). Random effects could be considered as another type of error. They can account for unobserved variables, but also for errors referring to different levels of a data set, for example levels of a geographically hierarchical data set. For instance when houses are nested within districts, then the lowest level refers to houses and the higher level refers to districts, and the resulting model is a typical multi-level model. Corrado and Fingleton (2012) and Dong et al. (2015) consider SAR models with added random effects to account for different types of data sets, such as grouped data, multilevel data and spatial panel data.

In this paper SLMs and SEMs are considered with an added measurement error but restricted to the lowest level, that is it is assumed that the true spatial process y i of unit i is unobserved and that the observed response z i has some measurement error, i.e. z i = y i + i with i ∼ N (0, σ 2 ). In the following the phrase measurement error refers to this situation. Most classical spatial econometric models do not distinguish between the measurement error i and the error of the spatial process y i . Spatial autoregressive models with an added measurement error term are not very common in the spatial econometric literature, although several authors have considered such models.

For example, Besag et al. (1991) considered a Poisson conditional autoregressive (CAR) model with measurement error using a Bayesian framework for estimation and Kang et al. (2009) a Gaussian CAR model with measurement errors using a pseudo-ML estimation approach. Another popular approximate Bayesian estimation method is the integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA) method (Rue et al. 2009;Bivand et al. 2015;Gomez-Rubio et al. 2017) implemented in the R package INLA, which currently provides the option to fit a CAR and a SLM with measurement error.

ML estimation of a SEM with measurement error has been considered recently by Burden et al. (2015). Because the corresponding log-likelihood is complicated, the authors used a reduced rank approach to allow estimation to be based on estimation of a spatial random effects (SRE) model (Cressie and Johannesson 2008), a flexible approach commonly used to model non-stationary covariance functions. This approach transforms the model into an SRE model and proceeds by fitting this SRE model, which is of order O(n) operations when n is the number of units. While estimation of SRE models is fast, the pre-processing is relatively slow and is based on some approximations, yielding approximate ML estimates only, see "Appendix B" for some details and an illustration.

In this paper, we propose an exact ML approach that is fast, without costly preprocessing as the reduced rank approach, and also does not rely on any approximations. We also propose a restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation method in order to obtain less biased variance parameter estimates. Our main focus in this paper is on computationally efficient exact ML/REML estimation of model parameters and not on prediction. When prediction is the main focus, see Goulard et al. (2017) for outof-sample and in-sample prediction of a classical SLM.

Section 2 introduces the two classical SAR models and the two extensions with measurement error. In Sect. 3, ML estimation of these extended models is discussed and various solutions are proposed, including the implementation of REML and the efficient calculation of standard errors. In Sect. 4, a small scale simulation study is conducted to compare the effectiveness of the methods and to allow comparison of REML and ML in terms of bias and coverage. Section 5 illustrates the models on a well known large data set on house prices with sample size n = 25,357 indicating that the measurement error models are potentially a more useful class of models compared to classical SAR models for this data set. In Sect. 6, we also provide a comparison in terms of computation time by comparing the times of the actual proposed ML/REML algorithms of this paper applied to some simulated data sets with the pre-processing needed for the reduced rank approach. It is also established that for sparse contiguity matrices based on a local neigbourhood the proposed methods are usually of order O(n 3/2 ) operations, confirmed in an empirical study.

div.head: Restricted maximum likelihood
div.p: The ML method does not take into account the degrees of freedom that are involved in estimating the fixed effects generally leading to biased variance components. REML accounts for these degrees of freedom by applying the ML method to a linear transformation Ky chosen so that KX = 0 and rank(K) = np, where p is the number of columns of the design matrix X which determines the mean μ = Xβ. A requirement for REML is that the distribution of Ky does not depend on the parameters governing the mean. A choice for K is the projection matrix P = I -X(X X) -1 X , see for example Verbyla (1990).

For the SEM, μ = Xβ and K = P. For the SLM, since μ = (A(ρ) -1 X)β, a natural choice would be to use P with X replaced by X = A -1 X, but the distribution of the transformation depends on the 'fixed effect' parameter ρ governing not only the (co)variance matrix but also the mean. Therefore strictly speaking REML cannot be applied to the SLM. Nevertheless, we still apply this REML procedure termed 'Pseudo-REML' (PREML) for the SLM. In a similar context when fitting linear models with nested errors for probability linked data such a PREML procedure has been applied by Samart and Chambers (2014). It was shown in an empirical study that the PREML method performs well and leads to improved estimation of variance parameters. Lindstrom and Bates (1988) simplified REML estimation by adding -1 2 log | X -1 X| to L and maximised the expression. The term simplifies to

div.head: Simulation study
div.p: We conduct an empirical simulation study for both models, the SEM-M and SLM-M. The parameters are set to σ 2 y = 1, σ 2 = 2, β 0 = 1 (intercept) and β 1 = 5 (slope). The spatial dependence parameter is set to ρ = -0.5, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9 in order to investigate the effect of negative and positive (low, medium and large) spatial correlation on the estimation. The covariate associated with β 1 is sampled from N (0, 1). We use the contiguity matrix from the Corrected Boston Housing Data provided by the R package spdep (Bivand 2017), which was collected by Harrison and Rubinfeld (1978). It contains n = 506 units, a size that makes the simulation study feasible.

Empirical mean estimates for parameters of the SLM are found in Table 3 and the empirical coverage of the model parameters of 95% Wald-type confidence intervals are found in Table 4. The "Appendix A" shows the results for the SEM-M in Tables 7, 8, 9, and 10.

Identifiability problems of the measurement error process have been mentioned by Kang et al. (2009) for the CAR model. A similar identifiability problem exists for the SEM-M, in particular for small to medium ρ. For example for ρ = 0.5, approximately 20% of the 10,000 simulated data sets have σ 2 ≈ 0 that leads to inflated values of σ 2 y . When removing these 20%, the results of the empirical means presented in Table 8 Table 3 Empirical mean of ρ, σ 2 y , σ 2 and β estimates over 10,000 simulations for the SLM-M model with n = 506, σ 2 y = 1, σ 2 = 2 and β 0 = 1 and β 1 = 5 ρ = -0.50 ρ = 0.10 ρ = 0.50 ρ = 0.90 show a much smaller bias for ρ = 0.5 and ρ = 0.9 and the results of Table 10 show improved coverages for ρ = 0.5 and ρ = 0.9. In conclusion, the methods seem to perform as expected, but they also show that separation/identification of the two processes is not always easy, particularly for small ρ. Clearly for ρ = 0, σ 2 and σ 2 y are not identifiable and only the sum σ 2 + σ 2 y can be estimated. In our simulation study, the effect of n was not investigated. It is expected that smaller n would lead to bigger identifiability issues, whereas larger n is expected to lessen the problem, as statistical accuracy is generally improved by increased n.

div.head: Example
div.p: The Lucas County (Ohio, USA) house price data consist of n = 25,357 observations of single family homes sold in the period 1993-1998. A full description is available in the Spatial Econometrics toolbox for Matlab, see http://www.spatial-econometrics. com/html/jplv7.zip. The data set is part of the R package spdep (Bivand 2017). The data have been used by Bivand (2010) to compare several types of software to fit spatial regression models and he used log house price (log( price)) as the response variable and the explanatory variables: powers of age (age, age 2 and age 3 ), log lot size in square feet (log(lotsi ze)), number of rooms (r ooms), the logarithm of the total living area in square feet (LT A), number of beds and an indicator for each of the years 1993-1998 (syear). We also use the same row-normalised sparse contiguity matrix W as used by Bivand (2010). For fitting the various models, we use a single core of a high performance cluster with CPU Type: Intel Xeon E5-2620 v2 -2.10GHz.

Table 5 shows the ML estimates and the time needed for the SLM, SEM, SLM-M, and SEM-M for the house price data set. The R package spdep (Bivand 2017) only provides ML estimates for the SLM and the SEM and therefore the table does not show REML but ML estimates for SLM-M and SEM-M for comparison purposes. Due to the large n, the difference in estimates between ML and REML is minimal. Both the SLM-M and SEM-M took longer than their counterparts without measurement error process. The reason why the SEM and SLM took far less time is that the underlying optimisation problem is one-dimensional (the concentrated log-likelihood depends only on ρ) and such problems can be solved quickly without numerical differentiations. In fact the package spdep uses the R function optimise() which is very fast for such onedimensional optimisation problems. REML and ML for SEM-M and SLM-M require solving a two-dimensional optimisation problem. We apply numerical differentiation which in turn needs many more evaluations of the log-likelihood, leading to increased calculation times. Table 5 also shows the number of evaluations of the log-likelihood. For the SEM-M, 145 such evaluations were needed and for the SLM-M 86 and this explains the increased time needed for fitting. For comparison purposes, our experience with fitting SEM and SLM using optimise() and using our own R code showed that only about 10-20 function evaluations are needed, explaining the 3.4 s for the SLM and 7.0 s for the SEM of the package spdep. For comparison purposes we also fitted the SLM-M with the R package INLA. The model fitting took approximately 209 s on the same computing machine, however this time includes the calculation of some summary statistics and marginal distributions. It appears the proposed ML algorithm is faster than the current implementation of the approximate Bayesian method.

The results are also interesting application-wise. When comparing the SLM and SEM using the log-likelihood, the results suggest that the SLM is the better model with L = -7670.36. However, when a measurement error term is added to the model, then the SEM-M is the best model with L = -6212.70. The underlying spatial process has a high spatial correlation with ρ = 0.9867 and a small variation of σ 2 y = 0.0004. The measurement error variance is σ 2 = 0.0685. The estimated ρ is close to one, however as long as ρ = 1 the covariance matrix is defined, in fact also any value of (Li et al. 2012). A possible explanation is that house prices are strongly determined by the local standard which depends on such explanatory variables as the number of bedrooms. For example, for a four bedroom house the area based (local) house price with similar features, which is set by the local market conditions, is almost fixed with hardly any variation and known by all local real estate agents. The actual selling price, however, varies from the market price depending on the buyer and the vendor (subject-specific variation) and this is captured by the measurement error. For example, some vendors need an urgent sale while others can afford waiting to obtain a potentially higher price.

div.head: Complexity comparisons
div.p: The calculation of eigenvalues is known to be computationally demanding. While complexity of matrix multiplication, inversion, the calculation of the determinant, the calculation of all eigenvalues and the Cholesky decomposition are all approximately O(n 3 ); for certain operations some optimal methods can do better. For example matrix multiplications can be achieved in O(n 2.38 ) operations (Villard and Thome 2002).

In practice sparse matrices, such as W for the house data set, allow much faster calculation, in particular this applies to the Cholesky decomposition and matrix multiplications. While the Cholesky decomposition requires n 3 /3 arithmetic operations for dense matrices, the complexity of the Cholesky decomposition is usually reduced to O(n) for temporal, O(n 3/2 ) for spatial and O(n 2 ) for spatio-temporal Gaussian Markov random fields (GMRF) (Rue and Held 2005, Ch. 2), for which a Cholesky factor has to be calculated for the sparse precision matrix Q = -1 . These time savings due to the sparseness of matrices usually apply to a much lesser extent to the spectral decomposition and matrix inversions. This explains why the proposed method (avoiding spectral decomposition and inversion of n × n matrices) is 'fast' for the house data set in the previous section.

Consider a regular grid of size √ n × √ n comprising n units. On this grid only the local neighbourhood is considered, such that two units are neighbours if W i j > 0 and otherwise W i j = 0. This is sometimes called the W neighbourhood. Based on a result by George and Liu (1981, Ch. 8) for a nested dissection ordering algorithm, Rue and Held (2005) established that the Cholesky factorisation of a precision matrix Q of a GMRF based on a local neighbourhood of a regular √ n × √ n grid has a complexity of order O(n 3/2 ) operations and that the Cholesky factor has at most O(n log n) non-zero entries. The result by George and Liu (1981, Ch. 8) also showed that any ordering algorithm requires at least O(n 3/2 ) operations and that the Cholesky factor has at least O(n log n) non-zero elements, establishing the optimal asymptotic bounds for the numeric operations and memory. Our proposed algorithm requires the calculation of the Cholesky factorisation of AA , see Sect. 3.1, or equivalently of the precision matrix Q of a standard SAR model
div.formula: Q = ω -1 I -ρ(W + W ) + ρ 2 WW = ω -1 AA
div.p: with contiguity matrix W (for a standard SAR model Q = ω -1 A A with contiguity matrix W).

In general Q is less sparse than W. Mukherjee et al. (2014) referred to the neighbourhood of a SAR model as the G neighbourhood where two units i and j are neighbours, when i and j are W-neighbours (referring to the term W + W in the matrix Q), or if they have a common neighbour k (referring to the term WW in matrix Q). When the W-neighbourhood is defined by centered (2 p + 1) × (2 p + 1) squares on a regular lattice, all G neighbourhoods are centered (4 p + 1) × (4 p + 1) squares (Mukherjee et al. 2014), see for example Fig. 1 with p = 1. We conclude that the Cholesky factorisation of Q is still of order O(n 3/2 ), because the G-neighbourhood still constitutes a local neighbourhood.

For illustration purposes, let us consider two types of adjacency matrices, where in both cases the 8 nearest neighbours are considered ( p = 1), see Fig. 2. In case (i) all n units are observed and in case (ii) only a 10% sample is available, meaning that the number of neighbours per unit within the 10% sample is usually smaller than 8. For the house data set, not all house prices are observed and the average number of observed neighbours is around 3-4 (< 8) for each observed unit. The setting in case (ii) also results in approximately 3-4 neighbours in average.

Various modern Cholesky methods for sparse matrices are implemented in many modern computer packages, for example the R package Matrix (Bates and Maechler 2017) and Matlab. To verify practically the complexities, we generate for a range of values of 100 ≤ n ≤ 1,000,000 the W matrices and perform the operations required for our approach: the calculation of AA (denoted by AAt), the Cholesky decomposition of AA (denoted by Cholesky using the R command Cholesky), the updated Cholesky decomposition of AA when θ I with θ = 2 is added (using the R command update, denoted by Cholesky update). For completeness, we also added the main operations needed for the pre-processing of the reduced rank approach, see "Appendix B": the calculation of the matrix B from X and W (B), all eigenvalues and vectors of B (EIGEN B), the 25 largest absolute eigenvalues of B (EIGEN B 25) using the R interface of the ARPACK (Lehoucq et al. 2015) software and the calculation of C (C). The matrix X is a dense random n × 10 matrix with entries from N (0, 1), representing a matrix of covariates.

For all of the sparse matrix operations the R package Matrix was used, unless otherwise stated. To verify results across platforms the Cholesky factorisation (as the most computationally demanding operation) has also been calculated using the Matlab routine "chol" for comparison purposes (denoted by Matlab chol). As this Matlab command usually does not apply an ordering algorithm we applied beforehand the Matlab routine "amd" performing the approximate minimum degree algorithm (Davis 2006), which is also used by default by the R routine Cholesky. This combination of chol and amd is denoted by "Matlab chol amd".

The results of the median times in seconds of up to 5 runs of some selected operations can be found in Fig. 3 for scenarios (i) and (ii). The calculation of all eigenvalues was limited to n = 20,000 and of all other operations to n = 1,000,000 as the time and the amount of memory exceeded feasible figures for larger values of n.

From these plots, the approximate complexities were determined by assuming that the time needed for each operation has the form TIME = b × n a + c × n = O(n a ) with a ≥ 1. The term c × n was added because some operations, like the ordering algorithms, are usually of order O(n). In practice the computation times differ for each run on a computer and an error term has to be accounted for. To obtain the parameters and in particular the coefficient of interest a, the method of weighted least squares with weights TIME -1 was applied to account for an increasing variance of the error term for increasing n.

For case (i) the results for n < 2000 were omitted for the estimation of a, as only from log 10 (n) ≈ 3.3 the curves have the shape of a line (the value a is approximately indicated by the slope of the line). Similarly for case (ii) only times for n > 20,000 were considered. The results of the coefficient a are found in Table 6. They indicate that the operations proposed in this paper needed for fitting the SLM-M and SEM-M are at most O(n 3/2 ) confirming the theoretical result by George and Liu (1981, Ch. 8) and the general experiences for spatial data by Rue and Held (2005). For case (ii), the complexity appears even lower, closer to O(n) than to O(n 3/2 ).

Interestingly the Matlab chol routine only appears to have complexity O(n 2 ), which is similar to using the R command chol without showing these latter results. For the methods Cholesky, update and Matlab chol amd the approximate minimal degree (amd) algorithm (Davis 2006) is used, reducing the operations of the Cholesky factorisation and explaining the reduced complexity of these methods. The O(n 2 ) operations for the Matlab chol routine and the R command chol can be explained by not applying such an ordering algorithm and is outlined next. For band matrices with bandwidth p, Rue and Held (2005, Ch. 2) showed that the Cholesky factorisation only requires O(np 2 ) operations. For a √ n × √ n grid the units can be ordered to have bandwidth p = √ n and O(np 2 ) = O(n 2 ) applies (Rue and Held 2005, Ch. 2). For our set-up, the units are already ordered such that W is already a band matrix with bandwidth p = √ n, and so WW and AA are band matrices with bandwidth 2 p = 2 √ n still leading to O(n 2 ). Notice it can be shown that WW is a band matrix with bandwidth 2 p if W is a band matrix with bandwidth p. The complexity for case (ii) appears lower because the bandwidth due to sampling appears less than √ n. For the reduced rank approach, EIGEN B 25 is around O(n 2.9 ) for type (i) and O(n 2.1 ) for type (ii), and the complexity for matrix B is around O(n 2.5 ). Overall the complexity for the reduced rank approach appears to be O(n 2 ) or higher, as the operation with the highest complexity determines the overall complexity of the approach. O(n 2 ) is also intuitively anticipated, because obtaining a fixed number of eigenvalues from the set of n eigenvalues should reduce complexity by factor n from approximately O(n 3 ) to O(n 2 ). For a similar problem, when solving AX = B for X with fixed n × n matrices A and B, generally O(n 3 ) operations apply (special case is the calculation of the inverse of A, i.e. X = A -1 when B = I), whereas when solving Ax = b for a vector x with fixed n × n matrix A and vector b usually O(n 2 ) operations apply.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We have provided fast ML and REML estimation methods for both SLM and SEM with an added measurement error term by re-expressing computationally complicated terms to ones that are computationally feasible for large data sets. From standard results of the Cholesky factorisation applied to matrices that have the form of spatial contiguity matrices, it can be concluded that our proposed exact (RE)ML method has an approximate complexity of O(n 3/2 ) operations, whereas the pre-processing of the reduced rank approach is at least O(n 2 ) based on numerical results. The proposed approach also appears to be faster than a popular approximate Bayesian approach, namely INLA. Popular model selection methods, such as Akaike information criterion, are likelihood based. The complexity of the proposed fitting approach is around O(n 3/2 ), hence the complexity of a model selection method for a finite number of models using such a likelihood based method for estimation will also be of the same complexity. For non-likelihood based methods a more thorough investigation could be considered.

In this paper we assume that the errors of the spatial process are homoscedastic, i.e. e ∼ N (0, σ 2 I). Often this assumption is violated and heteroscedasticity has to be accounted for, i.e. e ∼ N (0, σ 2 V) with usually diagonal matrix V with known/fixed elements. Here we did not consider this explicitly, however accounting for it is relatively simple, as it only requires changing the matrices/vectors y, X and Burden et al. div.head: B. Reduced rank approach
div.p: To fit the SEM-M, Burden et al. (2015) considered a reduced rank approach that relies on a spectral decomposition. Once this has been accomplished the computational complexity is reduced to that of a SRE model. The spectral decomposition of the matrix see formula (22) in Burden et al. ( 2015), is computationally intensive. The matrix P is the projection matrix defined in Sect. 3.2. The matrix U contains the eigenvectors of B and is a diagonal matrix with the eigenvalues of B on its diagonal. Notice that the matrix B is a first order approximation of the (co)variance matrix that is obtained from applying REML, ignoring second order terms. The decomposition can be written as
div.formula: B = P W + W P 2 = U U,(12)
div.p: where now 1 contains the largest r absolute eigenvalues and 2 the remaining nr , and where U j is the corresponding matrix containing the eigenvectors. The authors suggested then to use U 1 1 U 1 as an approximation to B and used this approximation to base estimation of the SEM-M on estimation of SREs. We use the house data set with n = 25,357, see Sect. 5, to illustrate the preprocessing times of the reduced rank approach. Instead of calculating all or a large number of eigenvalues we used Matlab and the R interface of the ARPACK software (Lehoucq et al. 2015) to calculate only the largest absolute r = 25 eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors. We would expect this process to take only a fraction of the time compared to calculating all n = 25,357 eigenvalues, presented in Fig. 4, which took 1 h and 36 minutes (min) using Matlab. However this process of calculating 25 eigenvalues took 54 min 40 s (s) with Matlab (using command 'eigs' and option 'largest magnitude') and 54 min 32 s with ARPACK (also option 'largest magnitude'), approximately two thirds of the time even though only ≈ 1/1000 (25/25,357) of the eigenvalues and vectors were calculated. Also the matrix B requires storage. In fact 4.9 GB of memory is required with R indicating that the calculation of B is limited by the available hardware. The objects of the proposed approach of this paper do not require much memory, for example W or the Cholesky decomposition of AA only require a couple of (up to 6) Megabytes.

The 54 min serves as a very optimistic lower bound for the time needed to fit this data set with the reduced rank approach. The SRE also has to be fitted, meaning that the total calculation time will clearly exceed this value. Figure 4 in Burden et al. (2015) demonstrates the effect of choosing different values of r ≤ 100 on ρ, showing the approximate nature of the method for various values of r .

Lesage and Pace (2009, p. 39) point out that for lagged models, as the SLM, the focus should rather be on impacts than on coefficients. To obtain distributions of some summary measures of impact, various methods are proposed by the authors, for example sampling the parameters from the asymptotic multivariate normal distribution of the ML estimates to obtain for each set a value of the impact measures. An alternative frequentist method would be to apply parametric bootstrap that would not rely naively on asymptotic normality for small sample sizes. The proposed computationally efficient method in this paper enables using parametric bootstrap, as for each bootstrap sample the parameter estimates have to be found quickly to make parametric bootstrap feasible.

Notice the spatial Durbin error model (SDEM) and the spatial Durbin model (SDM) contain the additional term WXθ compared to the SEM and SLM (Halleck Vega and Elhorst 2015). The SDM can be re-written as a SLM and the SDEM as a SEM by considering WX as a new covariate and θ as a new fixed effects parameter. In this sense, the present paper provides also computational efficient methods to fit those models with measurement error.
Future research aims at considering ML/REML estimation for other spatial econometric models with an added measurement error, such as spatial panel models for spatio-temporal data.
R code to fit the SEM and SLM with measurement error is available from the author's homepage http://www.uow.edu.au/~tsuesse/.
